title: Run JoinDependentFilterRule before DistributivityRule
hypothesis: q19 shape: WHERE (j AND a1 AND b1) OR (j AND a2 AND b2) OR (j AND a3 AND b3) with a* on table A, b* on table B, j the join equality. JoinDependentFilterRule (src/optimizer/rule/join_dependent_filter.cpp) is meant to derive (a1 OR a2 OR a3) AND (b1 OR b2 OR b3) and let filter pushdown push them to each scan, but it only fires when the ROOT expression is a CONJUNCTION_OR (Apply line 56-65, is_root only true on the top-level call in ExpressionRewriter::VisitExpression). DistributivityRule is registered earlier (optimizer.cpp:52 vs :69) and fires first, rewriting the root into AND(j, OR(...)); after that the OR is never root, so no derived filters. Evidence: EXPLAIN shows no filter on part scan; join builds 2M part rows and emits 2.14M rows (HASH_JOIN 0.87s, FILTER 0.39s, decompress PROJECTION 0.09s). Manually adding the derived filters to the SQL: join output drops to 2,672 rows, join 0.01s, filter 0.00s, total 0.783s -> 0.644s (~18%), same result 41150783.5184.
plan: In src/optimizer/optimizer.cpp Optimizer::Optimizer rule registration, move `rewriter.rules.push_back(make_uniq<JoinDependentFilterRule>(rewriter));` (line 69) to before DistributivityRule (line 52). Then the root OR is seen first: rule returns AND(original OR, derived), ApplyRules reruns (non-root) so Distributivity still factors j out of the inner OR; on the next fixpoint iteration root is AND so JoinDependent returns nullptr (no loop). Verify with EXPLAIN that the part scan gets an OR filter and lineitem gets an l_quantity OR filter (and the common shipmode/shipinstruct still pushed). If reordering causes trouble (e.g. other rules interfering, plan regressions), fallback: extend JoinDependentFilterRule::Apply to accept a root CONJUNCTION_AND, run the derivation on each CONJUNCTION_OR child, and append only derived conjuncts not already Equals() to an existing AND child (to guarantee fixpoint termination). Run the optimizer sql tests (test/optimizer/*join_dependent* if present) for results.
expected_gain: q19 ~15-20% (join/filter/decompress phases nearly vanish; scan remains)
generality: Any join query whose WHERE is a disjunction of per-branch conjunctions that each repeat the join key equality plus single-table predicates (common hand-written/ORM 'OR of cases' filters, TPC-H Q19, TPC-DS q13/q48-like shapes). Derived filters are implied by the original (sound), original predicate kept. Possible slowdown: extra redundant filter evaluation when derived filters are unselective (small cost).
risk: Low. Pure optimizer rule order; derived predicates are logically implied. Watch for volatile expressions (rule already skips) and for changed plan shapes in other tests.

title: Evaluate optional IN filters on dictionary strings inside scan
hypothesis: After the join fix, q19 is dominated by the lineitem TABLE_SCAN (4.15s cumulative) plus a separate FILTER for l_shipmode IN ('..','..') (0.36s) because the IN pushdown is marked 'optional' and re-evaluated above the scan on 15M rows. Applying it inside the scan on dictionary/FSST segments (comparing dictionary entries once) would drop the FILTER op and reduce rows emitted from 15M to 2.1M, cutting downstream decompression of other columns.
plan: Investigate how optional filters are created (grep 'optional' in src/planner/filter / dynamic/optional_filter) and whether dictionary_compression/fsst Select supports ConjunctionOr/InFilter; profile first.
generality: Scans with small IN lists on low-cardinality string columns.
risk: Medium; storage filter code, needs careful NULL/selection handling.

title: Linear-time union in scan ConjunctionOr filter
hypothesis: After E0001, q19 is dominated by the lineitem TABLE_SCAN (3.3s cumulative of ~3.6s). Isolated with dbe-tool sql: `count(*) WHERE l_quantity OR-of-3-ranges` takes 0.342s (scan 2.62s cumulative), while `l_quantity BETWEEN 9 AND 33` (same rows touched, one range) takes 0.099s (0.70s), and the shipinstruct eq filter alone takes 0.125s. So the OR table filter costs about 3.5x a plain range. The cause is in ColumnSegment::FilterSelection, case CONJUNCTION_OR (src/storage/table/column_segment.cpp:413-444). For every row that passes child k, it scans linearly through all rows already put into result_sel to remove duplicates. That is O(n^2) per vector: about 1000 passing rows of 2048 means about 10^6 compares per vector. Replacing it with a per-vector bitmap union is O(n) and should bring the OR filter close to the cost of a single range.
plan:
In ColumnSegment::FilterSelection CONJUNCTION_OR (src/storage/table/column_segment.cpp):
1. Allocate a local `bool matched[STANDARD_VECTOR_SIZE]` (or uint8), zeroed only for the indices in the incoming sel. sel indices are row offsets inside the scanned vector, so they are < STANDARD_VECTOR_SIZE. Add a D_ASSERT for this.
2. For each child: build `remaining_sel` holding the rows of the input sel that are not yet matched, in order. Skip the child if it is empty. Copy it into temp_sel and call FilterSelection(child) on it with remaining_count. Set matched[idx]=true for each passing idx.
3. Afterwards, iterate the original input sel in order and emit matched indices into result_sel. The output keeps input order (sorted) and has no duplicates. Then do sel.Initialize(result_sel) and approved_tuple_count = count.
This preserves semantics: the union of the rows each child passes. Evaluating later children only on unmatched rows is valid because a row already in the union does not need re-testing. Also look at whether ExpressionFilter or ZoneMap code in src/planner/filter/conjunction_filter.cpp has a similar quadratic union. Fix only if it is on the hot path.
expected_gain: q19: the lineitem scan OR filter drops from ~2.6s to ~0.8s cumulative. Expect q19 at -30..-50% (159ms -> ~90ms).
generality: Any scan with a pushed-down OR table filter on one column: OR'd ranges, OR'd equalities that are not converted to IN, and OR filters derived by JoinDependentFilterRule (Q19-like disjunctive queries). It is a pure algorithmic fix with no plan changes, so nothing should get slower. Output order becomes sorted by row position, which the AND path already produces.
risk: Low. The change is local. Points to watch: sel may be uninitialized (null pointer means identity), so use sel.get_index. Children may reorder or modify temp_sel, so copy before each child. NULL handling is unchanged because the children handle validity.

title: Dictionary-level filter evaluation for Dictionary-compressed string segments
hypothesis: The q19 lineitem TABLE_SCAN is still ~90% of the query (3.38s cumulative of 0.478s wall). l_shipinstruct and l_shipmode are stored with plain `Dictionary` compression and `Constant` validity (pragma_storage_info). An isolated `count(*) FROM lineitem WHERE l_shipinstruct='DELIVER IN PERSON'` costs 1.14s cumulative, about a third of the q19 scan. DictionaryCompressionFun::GetFunction (src/storage/compression/dictionary_compression.cpp:170) registers no `filter` callback. So StandardColumnData::Filter (standard_column_data.cpp:76) takes the fallback ColumnData::Filter: it emits a dictionary vector, then ColumnSegment::FilterSelection compares strings row by row through the dictionary sel (17-byte constant, so no inlined fast compare). DictFSST already has the fix (DictFSSTFilter, dict_fsst.cpp:180): evaluate the filter once on the dictionary entries (a handful per segment here), cache a bool per entry, then map each row via the dictionary sel. The Constant validity segment already has a filter (ConstantFilterValidity, numeric_constant.cpp:178), so once Dictionary has a filter the fast path will be taken.
plan:
1. In src/include/duckdb/storage/compression/dictionary/decompression.hpp, add to CompressedStringScanState: `unsafe_unique_array<bool> filter_result;` and `bool null_filter_result_initialized = false;` (mirror the dict_fsst scan state).
2. In src/storage/compression/dictionary_compression.cpp, add `DictionaryCompressionStorage::StringFilter(ColumnSegment&, ColumnScanState&, idx_t vector_count, Vector &result, SelectionVector &sel, idx_t &sel_count, const TableFilter&, TableFilterState&)`, ported from DictFSSTFilter:
   - Only when vector_count == STANDARD_VECTOR_SIZE and the dictionary was initialised.
   - Lazily build filter_result[dictionary_size] by running ColumnSegment::FilterSelection on `Vector(dictionary->data, 1, dictionary_size)` (slot 0 is NULL).
   - Unpack the bitpacked selection into sel_vec exactly as ScanToDictionaryVector does (including the start_offset shift).
   - Loop over the incoming sel (sel_count rows): idx = sel_vec[row]; slot 0 → evaluate the NULL entry lazily as DictFSST does; keep the row if filter_result[idx].
   - Write a new sel only if some rows were dropped. Set `result.Dictionary(dictionary, *sel_vec)` so later columns and the output still see the dictionary vector.
   - Otherwise fall back to StringScan + FilterSelection.
3. Register the filter. The CompressionFunction constructor has trailing optional args, so set `res.filter = ...` after construction (as dict_fsst.cpp:295 does).
4. Correctness guard: cache filter_result only when the filter tree (recurse through CONJUNCTION_AND/OR and OPTIONAL children) has no DYNAMIC_FILTER, BLOOM_FILTER or other filter whose result can change during the scan. For those, re-evaluate on the dictionary every vector (still cheap, since the dictionary is small), or fall back.
5. Check that ConstantFun::FiltersNullValues (numeric_constant.cpp:110) does not throw for any filter type that can now reach it on VARCHAR columns. Its default case throws InternalException; add the missing cases if needed (e.g. DYNAMIC_FILTER → filters_nulls=true conservatively is wrong; use filters_nulls=false, filters_valid_values=false, which keeps everything and is safe because the data filter already ran).
Verify with EXPLAIN ANALYZE count(*) WHERE l_shipinstruct = const (expect well below 1.14s cumulative) and with bench q19.
expected_gain: q19 -15..-25%: the shipinstruct equality is about 1/3 of scan CPU, and the optional shipmode IN on the same storage type also gets cheaper.
generality: Any scan with a pushed-down filter (equality, IN, range, LIKE-as-expression filter) on a low-cardinality VARCHAR column stored with plain Dictionary compression, which is very common in TPC-H/TPC-DS (flags, modes, statuses, categories). Regression case: a dictionary nearly as large as the vector (high-cardinality segment), where per-entry evaluation duplicates work. Bound it by taking the path only when dictionary_size <= vector_count, or let it be since it is amortised over the segment.
risk: Medium. Storage filter path: needs correct NULL slot-0 handling, the bitpacking start_offset shift, no stale cache for dynamic filters, and FiltersNullValues coverage. The DictFSST implementation is a proven template.

title: Skip all-optional ConjunctionAnd table filters in the scan filter loop
hypothesis: In q19 the lineitem scan (3.44s cumulative, about 85% of the query) carries a shipmode filter `optional: IN(..) AND optional: IN(..)`. Two optional pushdowns (filter_combiner.cpp:581 IN, and :659 OR-of-equals) on the same column get merged by TableFilterSet::PushFilter into a CONJUNCTION_AND. RowGroup::CheckZonemap (row_group.cpp:626) marks a filter always-true only when its top-level type is OPTIONAL_FILTER. So this AND stays active, and every 2048-row vector runs the column through ColumnData::Filter: a full decode of the shipmode Dictionary column, followed by FilterSelection calls on OptionalFilter children that do nothing. If the filter were skipped, the column would be fetched with Select on the few surviving rows (about 3 per vector in q19). Same-build A/B with `count WHERE l_quantity<2 AND l_shipinstruct=c AND l_shipmode IN(a,b)`, with and without an extra `(l_shipmode=a OR l_shipmode=b)` that produces the AND-of-optionals: scan 3.47s vs 3.03s, then 2.74s vs 2.25s cumulative (-13..-18%), with the same result rows. The upper FILTER operator re-checks the predicate anyway, so skipping it per row is correct.
plan: In src/storage/table/row_group.cpp RowGroup::CheckZonemap: keep the existing prune check (CheckStatistics on the AND still prunes row groups). Add a static helper IsPurelyOptional(const TableFilter&). It returns true for a filter_type==OPTIONAL_FILTER that is NOT a SelectivityOptionalFilter (check with dynamic_cast<const SelectivityOptionalFilter*> == nullptr; that class can actually filter, e.g. the BF and min/max dynamic filters), and for a CONJUNCTION_AND whose children are all IsPurelyOptional (recursive). Leave the existing top-level OPTIONAL_FILTER branch unchanged. Add `else if (filter.filter_type == CONJUNCTION_AND && IsPurelyOptional(filter)) filters.SetFilterAlwaysTrue(i);`. SetFilterAlwaysTrue already clears column_has_filter, so the column is then fetched via Select (scan_state.cpp:101). Include duckdb/planner/filter/selectivity_optional_filter.hpp and conjunction_filter.hpp. Optionally also make TableFilterSet::PushFilter (src/planner/table_filter.cpp) skip pushing an OptionalFilter whose child equals an existing optional child, to dedupe; keep that secondary. Verify with EXPLAIN ANALYZE of q19 (the lineitem scan should drop clearly) and with bench.
expected_gain: q19 -8..-15% (lineitem scan is about 85% of time; the microbench shows -13..-18% scan time)
generality: Any scan where two or more optional (zonemap-only) pushdowns land on the same column: IN lists combined with OR-of-equals, IN plus top-N filters, or derived OR filters from JoinDependentFilterRule. Today these needlessly force a full decode of the column per vector. No query should get slower: the skipped filter was a no-op per row. SelectivityOptionalFilter (BF/min-max dynamic filters) is excluded, so selective dynamic filtering is untouched.
risk: Low. One branch in CheckZonemap. The main hazard is accidentally treating a SelectivityOptionalFilter as purely optional, which would disable BF filtering (performance only, still correct because the join re-checks). Correctness is preserved because optional filters are always re-evaluated by the FILTER above the scan.

title: Cost-aware initial scan filter order: run Bloom/dynamic join filters after cheap constant predicates
hypothesis: Most of q19's time is the lineitem TABLE_SCAN (4.05-6.18s cumulative, ~85%). Standalone A/Bs in one dbe-tool session show the Bloom-filter join filter on l_partkey is the most expensive filter per row: BF-only scan 2.44s cum (349ms wall), shipinstruct-eq + quantity-OR without BF 1.57s (204ms), all three together 2.09s (286ms). Adding cheap selective predicates made the scan cheaper because less hashing was done. ExpressionHeuristics::Cost(const TableFilter&) (src/optimizer/expression_heuristics.cpp:225) gives OPTIONAL_FILTER/DYNAMIC_FILTER a cost of 0, so the l_partkey filter AND(opt>=, opt<=, opt BF) costs 5. That ties with the VARCHAR equality (ExpressionCost(VARCHAR,1)=5). EXPRESSION_FILTER falls to default 1000. The TableFilterSet map is keyed by scan column index, and the l_partkey column comes before l_shipinstruct. GetInitialOrder's sort on 4 elements is an insertion sort and keeps that order, so the initial permutation is [shipmode(always-true), partkey-BF, shipinstruct, quantity]. That means the BF hashes and probes all ~60M rows instead of the ~25% that pass shipinstruct. AdaptiveFilter (src/execution/adaptive_filter.cpp) can only fix this with random swaps judged on noisy 10-vector wall timings. One of the 3 swap slots involves the always-true shipmode filter, so those swaps are no-ops. Giving the BF a realistic, higher cost, and giving SelectivityOptionalFilter its child's cost, puts the BF after cheap comparisons from the first vector.
plan:
In src/optimizer/expression_heuristics.cpp, ExpressionHeuristics::Cost(const TableFilter &filter):
(1) case BLOOM_FILTER: return a hash-plus-probe cost, e.g. 50. That is above simple constant comparisons (1-5) and below generic expressions.
(2) case OPTIONAL_FILTER: if dynamic_cast<const SelectivityOptionalFilter *>(&filter) succeeds (include duckdb/planner/filter/selectivity_optional_filter.hpp), return Cost(*child_filter), because it really filters. A plain OptionalFilter stays 0, since it is skipped anyway.
(3) Optional, only if (1)+(2) alone do not reorder q19: EXPRESSION_FILTER returns Cost(*expr_filter.expr) via the existing Expression cost instead of 1000. Then a numeric OR-of-ranges (~104) is no longer treated as maximally expensive.
Keep DYNAMIC_FILTER at 0. Change nothing in AdaptiveFilter.
Verify with an A/B on the same build (temporarily switch the new branch on and off, or compare against the current best with bench run twice): the q19 lineitem scan cumulative time in `dbe-tool profile q19.m0`, then bench q19. Also sanity-check `SELECT sum(l_extendedprice) FROM lineitem WHERE l_partkey IN (SELECT p_partkey FROM part WHERE p_size<=5 AND p_brand='Brand#45')` (BF-only), so a scan where the BF is the only filter is unaffected.
expected_gain: q19: if the BF currently runs first on all rows, moving it after the 25%-selective string equality should cut BF hash/probe work ~4x. Estimate -10..-25% q19. It is 0% if AdaptiveFilter had already converged to that order (then retire, and note that ordering is not the bottleneck).
generality: Any scan probing a hash-join build where the scan also has cheap local constant predicates: star joins, TPC-H Q3/Q5/Q9/Q10/Q12/Q19-like shapes. This affects only the initial filter permutation, and AdaptiveFilter can still swap at runtime. It could get slightly slower when local predicates are unselective and the BF is very selective, but SelectivityOptionalFilter and adaptive swaps limit that. Results cannot change, because filter order does not affect correctness.
risk: Low. It only reorders conjunctive table filters, and all of them are evaluated anyway. dynamic_cast on TableFilter is polymorphic and safe. The main risk is no measurable gain within bench noise (~5-10%).

title: Skip pure-optional ConjunctionAnd scan filters (zonemap-only) in the per-row filter loop
hypothesis: Live `dbe-tool profile q19.m0` shows the lineitem TABLE_SCAN carrying `optional: l_shipmode IN (...) AND optional: l_shipmode IN (...)`: a CONJUNCTION_AND whose children are both plain OptionalFilter (zonemap-only, never removes rows; the real shipmode check is the FILTER above the scan, 82,782 -> 11,797 rows). RowGroup::CheckZonemap (row_group.cpp:626) only marks a filter always-true when its top-level type is OPTIONAL_FILTER, so this AND is evaluated per vector: ColumnData::Filter fully decodes l_shipmode (Dictionary VARCHAR) for all ~60M rows and runs no-op OptionalFilter::FilterSelection twice. Because the column counts as a filter column (column_has_filter), it never takes the cheap Select path (row_group.cpp:809-819), which would fetch only the ~83k surviving rows. E0003 measured a pass-everything filter on a Dictionary column at ~0.46s of ~2.7s cumulative scan time, so this pure overhead is roughly 10-15% of the dominant operator (scan 5.84s cumulative of 0.616s total in the profile).
plan: In src/storage/table/row_group.cpp RowGroup::CheckZonemap: add a static helper IsZonemapOnlyFilter(const TableFilter &f) that returns true when f is OPTIONAL_FILTER and NOT a SelectivityOptionalFilter (src/include/duckdb/planner/filter/selectivity_optional_filter.hpp, a final subclass with the same filter_type that DOES filter rows: BF and min/max dynamic join filters). Tell them apart with dynamic_cast/typeid, or with a small virtual on OptionalFilter (e.g. `virtual bool IsZonemapOnly() const { return true; }`, overridden to false in SelectivityOptionalFilter). It also returns true when f is CONJUNCTION_AND and every child satisfies it (recursively). Replace the `filter.filter_type == OPTIONAL_FILTER` test at line 626 with `filter.filter_type == OPTIONAL_FILTER || IsZonemapOnlyFilter(filter)`, keeping the existing behaviour for a top-level OPTIONAL_FILTER exactly as is. Zonemap pruning via CheckZonemap still runs first (line 622), so row-group pruning is unchanged. SetFilterAlwaysTrue already clears column_has_filter, so the column moves to the Select path automatically. Verify: the profile/EXPLAIN still shows the filter; bench q19; check that a query with a l_partkey dynamic AND (BF) still filters (the scan output row count stays at ~83k, not 15M).
expected_gain: q19 ~5-12% (removes a full decode of one Dictionary VARCHAR column and two no-op filter passes per vector over 60M rows in the dominant scan)
generality: Any scan where pushdown produces an AND of optional (zonemap-only) filters on one column, e.g. IN lists or OR-of-equalities pushed as optional, or duplicated pushdowns from derived OR filters (JoinDependentFilterRule). Correctness is unaffected: OptionalFilter never removes rows, and the original predicate is always kept in a FILTER above the scan. Nothing should get slower; the only behaviour change is skipping no-op per-row work.
risk: Low. The main risk is accidentally classifying SelectivityOptionalFilter (BF/min-max) as zonemap-only. That would not give wrong results (the join re-checks keys) but would lose the join-filter speedup. Guard it explicitly and check that the q19 scan output row count is unchanged.
